```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = FALSE)
```

Shiny's `ExtendedTask` is the standard way to run slow work off the session
thread. shinyasync does the same job through a smaller API: each async
reactive is a cancellable task modelled on `ExtendedTask`, on the same mirai
daemons. This
vignette writes the same app both ways, one piece at a time, so you can see
what the layer removes and what it costs.

The running example is the surf forecast dashboard from
[shinyasync-example](https://github.com/dawiegriesel/shinyasync-example).
`fetch_marine()` and `fetch_wind()` call Open-Meteo for a spot and return a
data frame of hourly conditions; `score()` combines the two into a surf score.
They are plain functions defined in the app's `R/` directory.

```{r setup}
library(shiny)
library(mirai)
library(shinyasync)
```

## The pool

Both run on mirai daemons. With `ExtendedTask` you start and stop them
yourself; with shinyasync the first task starts a pool and the last session
to use it shuts it down. `pool_async()` is there to size it.

```{r pool-et}
# ExtendedTask
daemons(4)
onStop(function() daemons(0))
```

```{r pool-sa}
# shinyasync
pool_async(workers = 4)
```

The arguments of `pool_async()` pass through to `daemons()`, so a remote or
TLS-backed pool is set up the same way. If you already manage daemons, call
neither.

## A slow fetch from an input

The forecast depends on the selected spot. In plain Shiny it is
`reactive(fetch_marine(input$spot))`.

`ExtendedTask` takes a function, not an expression. Reactive reads inside it
are masked, so the values go in as arguments, an observer calls `invoke()`
when the input changes, and outputs read `result()`. mirai ships nothing it
is not given, so the helper is passed in by name too.

```{r fetch-et}
# ExtendedTask
swell_task <- ExtendedTask$new(function(spot) {
  mirai(fetch_marine(spot), spot = spot, fetch_marine = fetch_marine)
})
observe(swell_task$invoke(input$spot))

output$swell <- renderPlot(plot_swell(swell_task$result()))
```

```{r fetch-sa}
# shinyasync
swell <- reactiveAsync(fetch_marine(input$spot))

output$swell <- renderPlot(plot_swell(swell()))
```

`reactiveAsync()` reads `input$spot` on the session thread, where it
registers the dependency, and sends the value to the worker with the
expression. `fetch_marine()` and every function it calls are found by
analysing the expression and shipped with it. The result is a reactive, so
nothing else in the app knows a worker was involved.

If `fetch_marine()` were left out of the `mirai()` call above, the task would
fail on the worker with `could not find function "fetch_marine"`. The usual
fix is `everywhere(source("R/api.R"))` after `daemons()`; shinyasync's
equivalent is `pool_async(everywhere = )`, which is optional because tasks
ship what they need.

## Status and the previous value

Both report `"running"`, `"success"` and `"error"`, and both halt an output
that reads a task that has not run yet. The differences are in the first state
and in what happens to the previous value.

```{r status-et}
# ExtendedTask
output$status <- renderText(swell_task$status())    # "initial" before the first invoke
```

```{r status-sa}
# shinyasync
output$status <- renderText(status_async(swell))    # "idle" before the first run
```

`invoke()` clears the stored value, and while the task runs `result()` halts
with `cancelOutput = "progress"`: the output keeps whatever it last rendered,
greyed out, but a reactive that reads `result()` gets nothing. An async
reactive keeps its previous value while a new one computes, so the old
forecast stays on screen and can still be read by other reactives.
`has_value_async()` tells the first run, which wants a spinner, from a
refresh, which wants a note:

```{r note-sa}
# shinyasync
output$note <- renderUI({
  running <- status_async(swell) == "running"
  if (running && !has_value_async(swell)) icon("spinner", class = "fa-spin")
  else if (running) span(class = "text-muted", "Showing the previous forecast")
})
```

## A button, and cancelling

The Monte Carlo band around the score should only run on a click, and the user
should be able to stop it.

`ExtendedTask` has a good story for the button: `bslib::input_task_button()`
and `bind_task_button()` disable the button while the task runs, with no code
in the server. It has no story for cancelling. The task does not expose its
mirai, so to stop it you keep a reference yourself, and `stop_mirai()` then
resolves the task with an error:

```{r button-et}
# ExtendedTask
current <- NULL
sim_task <- ExtendedTask$new(function(spot, swell, wind) {
  current <<- mirai(simulate_band(spot, swell, wind), spot = spot, swell = swell,
                    wind = wind, simulate_band = simulate_band)
  current
}) |> bslib::bind_task_button("go")

observe(sim_task$invoke(input$spot, swell_task$result(), wind_task$result())) |>
  bindEvent(input$go)
observe(stop_mirai(current)) |> bindEvent(input$cancel)

output$band <- renderPlot(plot_band(sim_task$result()))
```

After the cancel click the status is `"error"`, `result()` throws
`20 | Operation canceled` into the output, and Shiny warns that the task
failed. Showing the previous band instead means catching that error and
storing the last good value in a `reactiveVal` of your own.

```{r button-sa}
# shinyasync
sim <- reactiveAsync(simulate_band(input$spot, swell(), wind())) |>
  bindEvent(input$go)
observe(cancel_async(sim)) |> bindEvent(input$cancel)

output$band <- renderPlot(plot_band(sim()))
```

`bindEvent()` works on an async reactive as on a plain one. `cancel_async()`
stops the worker, sets the status to `"idle"` and keeps the last band, so
`has_value_async()` stays `TRUE` and the output does not change until the
next click. A button that disables itself reads the status:

```{r button-ui-sa}
# shinyasync
observe(updateActionButton(session, "go", disabled = status_async(sim) == "running"))
```

## Inputs that change while a task runs

Drag the spot selector through three spots while a fetch is running.
`ExtendedTask` queues: the three invocations run one after another, each
occupying a worker, and the output settles on the third after all have
finished. A plain `reactive()` would only ever compute the latest.

```{r latest-sa}
# shinyasync
swell <- reactiveAsync(fetch_marine(input$spot))                        # cancels, runs latest
saved <- reactiveAsync(save_favourite(input$favourite), mode = "queue")  # runs every one

output$saved <- renderText(saved())
```

`reactiveAsync()` cancels the running fetch and starts the latest, as a
reactive would. `mode = "queue"` gives `ExtendedTask`'s behaviour for work
that must not be skipped, such as saving each spot the user marks as a
favourite. Like any `reactiveAsync()`, a queued one starts only once
something reads it, here the confirmation text. `observeAsync()` has no
queue mode: a dependency change cancels its running task.

## A task that depends on another

The score needs both forecasts. In plain Shiny it is
`reactive(score(swell(), wind()))`.

With `ExtendedTask` the score is a third task, invoked from an observer that
reads the first two. `result()` halts while a fetch is running, so the
observer never pairs a new swell with an old wind, which is right. But the
score task is not told: while both fetches run for the new spot it still
reports `"success"` and `result()` still returns the old spot's score, so a
status badge on the score says it is done when it is about to change, and
nothing downstream can tell the difference.

```{r chain-et}
# ExtendedTask
score_task <- ExtendedTask$new(function(swell, wind) {
  mirai(score(swell, wind), swell = swell, wind = wind, score = score)
})
observe(score_task$invoke(swell_task$result(), wind_task$result()))

output$score <- renderText(score_task$result())
```

```{r chain-sa}
# shinyasync
scored <- reactiveAsync(score(swell(), wind()))

output$score <- renderText(scored())
```

An async reactive that reads another one waits for it: while `swell` is
catching up with a new spot, `scored` keeps its previous value, reports
`"running"` for as long as either fetch does, and runs once on the settled
pair. The expression is the one you
would have written for `reactive()`.

## Side effects and fan-out

Writing each scored forecast to a cache is an observer in plain Shiny. With
`ExtendedTask` it is a task nobody reads, plus the observer that invokes it.

```{r observe-et}
# ExtendedTask
cache_task <- ExtendedTask$new(function(spot, scored) {
  mirai(write_cache(spot, scored), spot = spot, scored = scored, write_cache = write_cache)
})
observe(cache_task$invoke(input$spot, score_task$result()))
```

```{r observe-sa}
# shinyasync
observeAsync(write_cache(input$spot, scored()))
```

Ranking all ten spots on a click is one task per spot. With `ExtendedTask`
that is one task object per spot, each with its own invoke. shinyasync's
imperative pair is `reactiveValAsync()`, a reactive value whose setter takes a
mirai, and `mirai_async()`, which starts a mirai with the same capture as
`reactiveAsync()`:

```{r fanout-sa}
# shinyasync
ranked <- lapply(spots, function(spot) reactiveValAsync())

observe({
  for (i in seq_along(spots)) {
    ranked[[i]](mirai_async(fetch_and_score(spots[[i]], days = input$days)))
  }
}) |> bindEvent(input$rank)

output$ranking <- renderTable(do.call(rbind, lapply(ranked, function(r) r())))
```

## Modules and tests

Inside `moduleServer()` nothing changes for either: `ExtendedTask` is created
with the module's `input`, and `reactiveAsync()` captures the namespaced
`input` and the module's local functions like any other reactive. A module can
return the async reactive to its caller, as it would return a `reactive()`.

Testing is the same for both. `shiny::testServer()` has to let the worker
finish and let Shiny see the result, which takes a few lines of
`later::run_now()` and `session$flushReact()`; `vignette("testing")` has them.

## What the layer costs

shinyasync finds the reactive reads in the expression by looking at it, which
`ExtendedTask` never has to do. The limits follow from that, and the README
section "How dependency capture works" lists them. The ones you are most
likely to meet:

- Reads must appear literally in the expression. `input[[paste0("x", i)]]`
  or a read inside a helper function cannot be resolved; read it in a
  `reactive()` first.
- Every read is a dependency, even in a branch that is not taken, unless it
  is wrapped in `isolate()`.
- The task must be a mirai. `ExtendedTask` accepts any promise, so a
  `future`, `callr` or `httr2::req_perform_promise()` task needs
  `ExtendedTask`, or `reactiveValAsync()` fed by hand.
- `bind_task_button()` and the OpenTelemetry spans Shiny records for an
  `ExtendedTask` have no counterpart here yet.

## Summary

| | `ExtendedTask` | shinyasync |
|---|---|---|
| Written as | task object, invoking observer, `result()` reads | `reactiveAsync(expr)` |
| Reactive reads | passed as arguments | captured from the expression |
| Helpers on the worker | passed by name, or `everywhere()` | shipped automatically |
| Input changes while running | queued | cancelled and re-run (`mode = "queue"` to queue) |
| Previous value while running | cleared; output greyed out | kept; `has_value_async()` tells first run from refresh |
| Cancel | keep the mirai yourself; task ends in `"error"` | `cancel_async()`; status `"idle"`, value kept |
| Depends on another task | another task and observer | read it in the expression |
| Side effect | task nobody reads, plus observer | `observeAsync()` |
| Task source | any promise | mirai |
| Status values | `initial`, `running`, `success`, `error` | `idle`, `running`, `success`, `error` |
